title: Tony Abbott and Angus Taylor are pushing for "change", as did Trump, writes John Hewson
text:
Article text size: This control adjusts article text size. For broader accessibility options, please use your browser or device text scaling settings.

It is a global phenomenon that voters are looking for change. I have to ask, change to what? In this increasingly challenging world, on recent experience, it’s best to be careful what you wish for.

Presumably the desire is for better government. Hence, the approach should be to vote for the team that is capable of good and effective governance, with the experience and the policies to make a real difference. It should not be simply a popularity contest or a protest – the objective should be beyond simply expressing disappointment or grievance.

The new Liberal Party president, Tony Abbott, and leader Angus Taylor have recently focused heavily on this “need for change”, to get rid of what they call this “rotten Labor government”. Ironically, they share a record of election losses. Their time in government failed to address the big issues effectively, with their party preferring to kick the can down the road.

The presidency of Donald Trump in the United States and the prospect of a Nigel Farage prime ministership in the United Kingdom should serve as warning against a drift to the fringes. This is becoming a particularly relevant concern in Australia with the surging popularity of Pauline Hanson and One Nation and their tendency to get ahead of themselves in assuming a capacity to win government. There is little to suggest they will have the competence or the policies to form an effective one.

Trump must serve as the most concerning example of incompetent government. When he was emerging as a potential candidate, I expressed concern that his claim to the position was as a property developer and a reality TV star with The Apprentice. I argued a property developer mostly uses other people’s money, such that if the project is a success, the investors will profit, but if it fails, they lose. The nonsense propagated in his book The Art of the Deal was the basis of his election pitch to bring a “business approach and experience” to deliver better government – in his words, “to drain the swamp”, to “shake things up”, and so on. All this under the emotive pledge to “Make America Great Again”.

It is sad that the Liberals prefer a government led by the far right than by Labor. I guess some are dreaming of a coalition with One Nation rather than the spent force of the Nationals. The Coalition’s standing will continue to erode…

Trump has certainly not lived up to the heady promises he made. He now sits on top of an oligarchy that has mostly governed to the benefit of himself and a cabal of obscenely wealthy family and friends.

He has undermined the public service, preferring to appoint sycophants rather than qualified or experienced advisers. His domestic policy responses have been erratic, based on his prejudices rather than evidence-based analysis. He has undermined the congress and the justice system, and developed his own militia, in the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents who have caused the deaths of innocent Americans. He has compounded the cost-of-living crisis with his ill-conceived tariffs, deportations and budgetary initiatives. This also resulted in job losses and constrained growth.

It has been estimated that in his first administration alone he added $8.4 trillion to the national debt – a 39 per cent increase. He has added another 7.6 per cent increase in this term so far. There’s nothing really “great” in any of that. His performance has the hallmarks of irresponsible government, to the detriment of average Americans and to the US’s standing in the world.

On top of this domestic disaster, Trump’s ignorance and unpredictability has undermined what had been the global rules-based order. He ignored trade deals, alliances and national sovereignty, seriously destabilising the world economy, geopolitics and the essential global energy transition – making this an even more challenging time for all governments around the globe.

Farage in the UK has been operating as a “mini Trump”, running a particularly divisive strategy “to take our country back” with strong racist overtones and claims that “Britain is Broken, Britain needs Reform”. His popularity and thrust comes from his campaign, similarly race-based, to ensure the UK exited the European Union – Reform UK is a rebadging of the Brexit Party from 2019. This is not much of a base to demonstrate a capacity for competent government. Indeed, his Brexit campaign ignored the voluminous policy warnings concerning the possible trade and financial consequences – like Trump, he would pursue populism and prejudice rather than evidence.

Nevertheless, the polls suggest he leads the fastest-growing political movement in the UK. Farage has been most active signing up a host of former and sitting MPs, mostly from the Conservative Party, including cabinet ministers and backbenchers. It is a basket of scoundrels, most excited not at the prospect of real reform but of being on a winning team.

Like Trump, Farage is also very open to accepting large donations from wealthy individuals, conspicuously a £5 million “personal gift” from Christopher Harborne, a Thailand based cryptocurrency billionaire who claimed no strings were attached. The money, which Farage said was to cover the cost of his personal protection, was given before he became an MP after seven failed attempts. It was not declared in Farage’s register of members’ financial interests. Farage has not handled the controversy well, claiming a leak of personal information (that his phone was hacked by Russian spies), then exploitation by the “deep state”.

Harborne also made a £9 million donation to Farage’s Reform UK, making him the largest single living donor in the history of British politics. The Art of the Deal indeed.

The UK branch of Transparency International has reported the huge donations from Harborne are part of a trend that’s evolved over the past decade. In 2015, just 1 per cent of donations to political parties from individuals or companies were for £1 million or more; by the last general election in 2024, the proportion had climbed to 35 per cent.

The past year has seen the advent of an even more right-wing party, Restore Britain, led by Rupert Lowe, whom Farage kicked out. Lowe has attracted considerable financial and editorial support from tech mogul Elon Musk, via his platform X, at the expense of Farage.

The surge in support for Pauline Hanson and One Nation is a reflection of the Trump-Farage phenomena. Indeed, it seems Hanson has adopted their model. Although she claims hers is the party for working Australians, she too has her controversial billionaire backer, Gina Rinehart. Hanson has also sought to attract sitting and former MPs, and her emerging electoral strategy seems to be to win seats from both the Coalition and Labor.

According to recent polls, One Nation has overtaken the government in terms of primary votes, which has encouraged some to claim the far-right party could win the next election. However, the challenge for One Nation is to convert poll standings to seats in what promises to be some pretty tough contests. Preferences are as important as ever, and it is noteworthy that Coalition preferences helped One Nation to win several seats in the recent South Australian election, and handed One Nation victory in the Farrer byelection.

The recent Australian Financial Review, RedBridge Group and Accent Research poll has posited outcomes in terms of seats in the next federal election. It sees Labor with 76 seats, One Nation on 53 and the Coalition on 12. An allocation of preferences based on the South Australian election outcome would see an exchange of about 10 more seats to Labor from One Nation, with the Coalition unchanged at 12.

While Hanson and her colleagues have declared themselves “humble”, they have got ahead of themselves if they envisage Hanson after the next election actually leading the opposition, or even becoming prime minister. The party would be ill prepared for this elevation, to say the least, in terms of both policies and the skills and experience of their prospective team. The Coalition has lost the past two elections to Labor, as voters concluded they were not ready for government and had just been in government under Scott Morrison.

Despite their recent polling and electoral success, the organisation of the One Nation party is still subpar. This has been particularly clear in relation to candidate selection and vetting, where successful candidates in South Australia and Farrer have broken ranks on their key policy of immigration, and on some social issues. Most recently we saw a disagreement between Hanson and her new MP Barnaby Joyce over housing policy, showing a lack of understanding of policy positions.

I have no doubt much of the growing support for Hanson over the past 30 years has been because she provided a platform for protest and grievance over the broad performance of the two major parties. From the start, there was an undercurrent of racism in the support, particularly against Asian migration. This carried through into the resistance to the Voice referendum and anti-Muslim sentiment. People seemed to have assured themselves Hanson would never be in government and so agreeing with her grievances felt harmless – a vote for her was without serious consequence.

This surety of minimum consequences is fading as her popularity surges and trust in the major parties continues to wane. I suggest that as we get closer to the 2028 federal election, and she and her team are subjected to greater scrutiny, they will be found wanting on their proposed solutions to the many big issues that confront our nation. Poll popularity will not transfer easily to hard votes and seats.

In the meantime, the Coalition is panicking and Abbott and Taylor have committed to preference deals with One Nation, hoping to stem the tide. It is sad that the Liberals prefer a government led by the far right than by Labor. I guess some are dreaming of a coalition with One Nation rather than the spent force of the Nationals. The Coalition’s standing will continue to erode, opening opportunities that Hanson will try to exploit. Increasingly, though, I feel Australia will recognise she is not ready for government nor capable of the kind of global representation that Australians will want.

At least, this is my hope. May Ms Hanson never achieve her dreams.

John Hewson  is a professor at the ANU Crawford School of Public Policy and former Liberal opposition leader.
